dek: Two true steakhouses, eight secret cuts, and one neighborhood that knows how to eat.

slides.label: Midtown vs Harlem
slides.text: Midtown has a steakhouse on every corner. Harlem has *two true steakhouses* and a deep bench that quietly serves a serious cut.

slides.label: Why so few
slides.text: Chef Cisse told us plainly: *'We don't have that many of that in Harlem.'* That's why this list stays short and honest.

slides.label: Casa Ricardo
slides.text: *Casa Ricardo*, once Ricardo Steakhouse, has run 22 years in El Barrio. Porterhouse, skirt steak platter, Motown on the speakers.

slides.label: PB Brasserie
slides.text: Chef Elhadji Cisse came from Senegal at 17, started as a dishwasher, now owns four Harlem spots. His ribeye is *dry-aged*.

slides.label: 8 sleepers
slides.text: None of these call themselves a steakhouse. That's the point, the steak is the *sleeper* on the menu.

slides.label: Pick your craving
slides.text: *Vinatería's* steak au poivre, *Red Rooster's* steak frites, *Cocotazo's* bistec encebollado, cash only, El Barrio style.

slides.label: The verdict
slides.text: Downtown sells steak as *status*. Uptown it comes with rice and beans, a jazz trio, or a DJ who knows your song.

caption_instagram:
Best steakhouses in Harlem come down to two names, and that's the whole point.

Casa Ricardo has held down El Barrio for 22 years on porterhouse, skirt steak and Motown on the speakers. PB Brasserie's Chef Elhadji Cisse went from dishwasher at 17 to dry-aging ribeyes on 125th Street. He told us straight, 'We don't have that many of that in Harlem,' which is why the steakhouse count stays at two.

But the real list runs deeper. Vinatería's steak au poivre, Red Rooster's steak frites and Cocotazo's cash-only bistec encebollado all quietly out-cook rooms charging triple downtown.

caption_linkedin:
Harlem has almost no steakhouses, and that gap is the story. Search 'steakhouse near Harlem' and most results point to Midtown, the Upper East Side or Yankee Stadium.

Two operators filled that gap differently. Casa Ricardo has held its lane in East Harlem for 22 years by refusing to copy Midtown, serving porterhouse alongside skirt steak, rice and beans and Motown on the speakers.

PB Brasserie's Chef Elhadji Cisse arrived in New York from Senegal at 17, started as a dishwasher, and now owns four Harlem restaurants, including a brasserie built around dry-aged steak. His read on the market was simple: 'We don't have that many of that in Harlem.'

The demand doesn't disappear because no one served it well. It just waits for someone who understands the block.
